title: KV eviction wave & FlashFusion sensitivity — exploratory notes
content:
Summary:

Quick exploratory notebook capturing a handful of small experiments showing a reproducible latency/regression mode when paged KV eviction waves coincide with very small (1-4 token) microbatches and FlashFusion fused-op selection. Not fully root-caused but high signal for a cache/timing interplay.

Why I care:
- Several customer traces (see linked Linear issue INF-477) show 99.9% spikes during short responses (e.g., chat completions 10-40 tokens) that correlate with increased paging activity.
- Hypothesis: eviction-induced DMA/host<>device synchronization plus fused-kernel scheduling choices (FlashFusion path) cause transient kernel handoffs and stall the attention hotpath.

Testbed (quick):
- HW: 8x A100-40GB (nvlink enabled), single-GPU experiments pinned to one device for deterministic pockets; multi-GPU for cross-GPU NVLink tests.
- SW: runtime commit 4f2b3d (bundle 0.9.7), FlashAttention v2 shim, FlashFusion branch preview-ff-3.
- Models: llama-2-7b (hf trimmed), seq len 1024, per-request tokens sampled 1..64 (focus 1..16).
- Config: paged-KV enabled (page size 512MB), eviction threshold 75% free-slab, batching policy: continuous-batcher with microbatchers flush at 1ms and 8ms.
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency, kernel occupancy, stream wait times, GPU memcpy time, page-in/page-out counts, kernel selection logs.

Experiments + observations:

1) Baseline: no paging (large active KV slab) + FlashFusion enabled
- Microbatch sizes: 1, 4, 16.
- Result: stable latency; p99 ~ 12ms (1 token), p99 ~ 18ms (4 tokens), no unusual memcpy spikes.
- Kernel selection: consistently chooses fused-attn kernel (FF path).
- Note: warm-run, steady-state, KV hit rate > 99%.

2) Induce eviction wave (fill slab, then force background eviction)
- Method: artificially lower free slab and trigger background cleaner to start page-out sweep; simultaneously run microbatches with sizes 1..4.
- Observation: sporadic p99 spikes up to 160ms mostly for microbatch size 1 and 4. Spikes correlate with burst of page-out requests (NVMe->host->gpu movement).
- Kernel selection during spikes: log shows fallback from FF fused kernel to paged-safe FlashAttention path (non-fused) then back, with ~2-3 kernel handoffs per request.
- GPU memcpy: host->device memcpy time jumps (avg +8ms per token), stream serialization observed (stream 0 waits 6-12ms).

3) Disable FlashFusion (force legacy fusedops off), paged KV active
- Result: p99 spikes reduced but not eliminated; peak ~60ms.
- Interpretation: FlashFusion handoff amplifies stalls but is not sole cause; host<->device page movement contributes base cost.

4) Increase microbatch delay (coalesce short requests into 8-token batches) while eviction wave active
- Result: latency p99 drops dramatically (peak ~28ms).
- Note: coalescing hides DMA latency since memcpy amortized across more tokens and fused kernel selection stabilizes.

5) NVLink cross-GPU test (paged-KV split across GPUs, eviction on remote GPU)
- Result: higher tail (p99 up to 220ms) when page-ins require NVLink transfer. Kernel logs show blocking on remote memcpy and then kernel selection fallback.

6) Kernel-priming mitigation: introduce a tiny synthetic warmup kernel (null op) to keep fused kernel resident on SMs right after eviction starts
- Result: small improvement; p99 drops ~15% from eviction-only baseline. Not a full fix.

Hypotheses to explore further:
- Eviction wave causes asynchronous memcpy operations which create short-lived stream contention; fused kernel selection logic is sensitive to stream backpressure and toggles kernel variants mid-request. Those toggles induce extra synchronization points and amplify tail.
- Small microbatches are especially vulnerable because amortization is low and kernel handoff overhead is large relative to useful compute.
- NVLink transfers add additional jitter when remote pages are involved.

Immediate actionable experiments (next week):
- Add detailed per-request timeline tracing (host timeline + GPU stream timeline) to correlate exact sequence of cudaMemcpyAsync, kernel launches, and events. (PR: github PR in linked_artifacts already started).
- Modify kernel selection heuristic: add hysteresis/hold-time so once a fused kernel is chosen for a stream it doesn't flip back for O(10ms) unless explicit rejection reasons. Quick patch + bench.
- Try two-stage coalescing: tiny requests (1-3 tokens) wait up to 3ms to see if can be coalesced without violating latency SLO; measure p99 improvement vs p50 degradation.
- For paged KV, experiment with background prefetching tuned to predicted near-term keys (heuristic from recent trace samples) to reduce remote page-ins during short completions.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Capture a deterministic trace of a p99 spike with all telemetry on (include nvprof-like capture, but lightweight).
- Check PR 842 for existing kernel-selection logs parsing; update to include eviction-wave flag.
- Talk to SRE about running a controlled eviction wave on a small cluster to reproduce customer traces (Marco volunteered).
- Evaluate whether a QuickStop fallback (immediate return-on-error) would be better than kernel toggles for strict-latency customers.

Open questions:
- Can kernel selection be made per-stream (isolated) rather than per-request? Behavior differs across streams when memcpys are in-flight.
- Are there power-management interactions (GPU clock gating) when large memcpy bursts happen that increase kernel launch latency? Need perf counters on sm_efficiency and clocks.
- Is page size (512MB) too coarse for these workloads? Smaller pages reduce amount evicted but increase page-tracking metadata overhead.

Raw numbers (representative single-run snippets):
- Baseline (no paging) microbatch=1: p50=8.6ms p95=11.8ms p99=12.3ms
- Eviction wave + FF + microbatch=1: p50=9.4ms p95=30.2ms p99=160.7ms (12 spikes >100ms observed in 1k requests)
- Eviction wave + no-FF + microbatch=1: p50=9.0ms p95=22.1ms p99=59.8ms
- Eviction wave + coalesce(8) + FF: p50=17.1ms p95=21.8ms p99=27.9ms

Conclusions (working):
- There's a clear interplay between paged KV eviction, host<->device memcpy activity, and fused kernel selection that amplifies tail latency for very short requests.
- Mitigation strategies that look promising: coalescing, selection hysteresis, smarter prefetching, or changing eviction pacing.
- Quick wins: coalescing and hysteresis provide measurable p99 improvements with limited code surface.

Appendix: trace snippets / commands used
- trace capture: ./tools/trace_driver --model llama-2-7b --seq 1024 --tokens 1-16 --ttls 1000 --telemetry=full --out spike.trace
- eviction trigger: python tools/kv_slab_filler.py --target-free-percent 5 --hold 30s
- kernel logs: /var/log/serving/runtime/kernel-selector.log (filter: grep "switch-to" )

If anyone reading this wants to grab it: please ping me in #eng-serving-runtime or comment on SERV-1293. Will iterate on per-request timelines next.

-- Aisha
